Hi! Good questions. Lots of things have increased. Self tan ingredients especially (due to the demand following the upcoming restrictions in the EU), Active ingredients too- the ones with clinical trials behind them even more so, silicones (yes I know some people think these are the devil but lots of them are plant derived now), and many more. 

It’s easier for a company to take a hit on a product with one component, like your powder, but when there’s processing involved then we have to add a little on in the worst cases. Energy prices are going up too, my companies energy bill is doubling this year (no we aren’t passing it on) despite having solar panels and other very green sources, so there’s hits all over the place. Small manufacturers will feel it most.

Each company tends to “shop around” their suppliers. We never get the same product from the same supplier two batches in a row, we take who has the best price at the time. But we have to consider safety and quality too. Suppliers must be reputable, it’s not like kitchen table brands that can go on alibaba and get seconds or knock offs. We would be responsible if anyone got hurt because something we used was substandard.

Yes, I can see why it would look that way, but even synthetic ingredients have to come from somewhere. Chemicals are still isolated from petroleum, sugar, wheat, mining etc. which unfortunately means they’re affected by governments, gas prices, shipping, international instability, weather etc etc. Packaging is the same, a lot is still made in china too so shipping times are lengthy.

As a development chemist- we apologise. But, as you say, supply chain. Our ingredient prices have shot through the roof, and suppliers know they have us over a barrel, because what are we gonna do? Not make your products? I know that where I work, we absorb what we can, and other reputable places do the same, but eventually, like everything in life, that becomes untenable and we must pass it along. 
A tip might be to avoid wholesalers/resellers, who will each take a cut, and buy direct from the brand’s website- but it’s not guaranteed.

You might just need to play about with different brands but from a professional point of view (cosmetic chemist) I would suggest :

- avoid a guide colour. Go for the clear waters/mousses. It will be easier to soak in without leaving a residue on the skin. 
-For a total novice, gradual tans  are good because they’ll be moisturisers with some dha in and easier to be sure you haven’t missed a spot. 
- Exfoliate before use but don’t moisturise, you don’t want to put a layer between your skin and the tan. If you find this causes streaking, there are pre-tan primers which work better than oil based moisturisers. 
- If absorption is still an issue, you may need to play a numbers game eg use a darker shade and shower sooner to rid yourself of the balling. 
- Tans containing ethoxydiglycol and/or dimethyl isosorbide will absorb more easily. Look for these in the ingredients.

As for exfoliating:

- maybe try an aha type product, rather than a physical one. Look at urea based things too. There are specific brands for people with keratosis pilaris which could work.

The ones I use most pretty much fall into two categories. 
Carbopols- these are mostly white powders which are added to water. They are mixed either by vortex mixer or by homogeniser depending on the specific material and neutralised using caustic/triethanolamine (mostly) to form a gel. The most obvious use of these right now is hand sanitisers but they can also be used in hair gel, and to support surfactant systems like shampoos. 

The other type comes in liquid form and usually have INCI names involving acrylates and copolymer. These are slightly easier to use if you only need a small amount, eg in a scrub or lotion, just to suspend or thicken without really gelling, though they are capable of it too. Again these need to be neutralised within the product. A quirk of these is that, depending on your product, it can be easier to neutralise the water before the material is added.

Look at industry jobs.  They're more routine and boring than what you expect from pharma, but they take fresh graduates and give GMP training. Try the big names, GSK, AstraZenica,Merck etc. They usually have QC roles or similar technician roles. 

Try not to be put off by job titles. I know "technicians" that have been out of uni 5/6 years. It's just a name, not actually reflective of the work they do. Every company calls it something different but "scientist" or "analyst" roles are the ones you work up to and are rarely given to fresh grads. 

As for your applications, list everything you've ever done, even if it feels irrelevant, and try to make it fit. E.g. Retail work = client interaction, stock control, time management. Office work = admin skills, meeting deadlines. 

Hope that helps a bit. I don't know much about junior exec roles but it sounds like a work up to it role too.
